knowledge_point.title: Differentiating a Radical Function Using the Chain Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=-3x+7.$ Then $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}={u}^{-1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-\frac{1}{2}{u}^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{u}^{3}}}
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{u}^{3}}}\cdot (-3) \\  & =\frac{3}{2\sqrt{(-3x+7{)}^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: The slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3{x}^{2}-13x}}$ at the point where $x=-1$ is{{field-1}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=3{x}^{2}-13x.$ Then $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}={u}^{-1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-\frac{1}{2}{u}^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{u}^{3}}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6x-13.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{u}^{3}}}\cdot (6x-13) \\  & =-\frac{6x-13}{2\sqrt{(3{x}^{2}-13x{)}^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=-1} & ={(-\frac{6x-13}{2\sqrt{(3{x}^{2}-13x{)}^{3}}})|}_{x=-1} \\  & =-\frac{6(-1)-13}{2\sqrt{(3(-1{)}^{2}-13(-1){)}^{3}}} \\  & =\frac{19}{2\sqrt{{16}^{3}}} \\  & =\frac{19}{128}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{-3x+61}+2{x}^{3}$ at the point where $x=4.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

Let $f(x)=\sqrt{-3x+61}.$ We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=-3x+61.$ Then $f=\sqrt{u}={u}^{1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2}{u}^{-1/2}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (-3) \\  & =-\frac{3}{2\sqrt{u}} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2\sqrt{-3x+61}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the sum rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{3}{2\sqrt{-3x+61}}+6x^{2}.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=4} & =-\frac{3}{2\sqrt{-3(4)+61}}+6(4)^{2} \\  & =-\frac{3}{14}+96 \\  & =\frac{1341}{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: The slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+10x}$ at the point where $x=2$ is{{field-1}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=-{x}^{2}+10x.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=10-2x.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (10-2x) \\  & =-\frac{2(x-5)}{2\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+10x}} \\  & =-\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+10x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=2} & ={(-\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+10x}})|}_{x=2} \\  & =\frac{10-2(2)}{2\sqrt{-(2{)}^{2}+10(2)}} \\  & =\frac{6}{2\sqrt{16}} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
